title: Allocators and leaks
sub: Temp, TempJob and Persistent, how to find a forgotten Dispose, and why a long-lived buffer is allocated once
cards/0/title: The garbage collector does not see native memory
cards/0/body:
NativeArray, NativeList, NativeReference and the other native containers live outside the managed heap. The struct itself is a pointer, a length and (in the Editor) a safety system handle; a copy of the struct points to the same memory. That is exactly why you can hand them to a job.

The flip side: the garbage collector never frees that memory. Every allocation has to be closed with Dispose(), otherwise it is a leak that will not go away on its own.

When you create a container you pick an allocator. It decides how fast the allocation is, how long the memory lives and which checks Unity runs for you.
cards/1/body:
Allocator.Temp is the fastest. Every frame the main thread creates a Temp allocator and releases it in full at the end of the frame; each job gets its own Temp per thread, released at the end of the job. You do not need to call Dispose() — it does nothing.

Allocator.TempJob is slower than Temp and faster than Persistent. It is for data that goes into a job. Free it within 4 frames, or the Editor complains: the Unity Manual calls it a warning, the Collections docs say native containers throw an exception.

Allocator.Persistent is a wrapper over malloc: the slowest allocation and no lifetime checks at all, the memory lives until you call Dispose(). “Slow” is about allocating, not about access: reading and writing that memory is just as fast.
cards/1/flow/0: Temp → until the end of the frame or job
cards/1/flow/1: TempJob → into a job, Dispose within ≤ 4 frames
cards/2/q: A one-off buffer: filled in Update, processed by a job and read in LateUpdate of the same frame. Which allocator?
cards/2/options/1: Allocator.Temp — it lives until the end of the frame anyway
cards/2/options/2: Allocator.Persistent — it is the most reliable
cards/2/options/3: Any: the allocator only affects speed
cards/2/explain: The data goes into a job and lives for less than 4 frames — that is exactly TempJob. Main-thread Temp cannot be passed into a job. Persistent here is the slowest allocation with no lifetime check: forget the Dispose and you get a silent leak.
cards/2/wrong/1: Main-thread Temp memory cannot be passed into a job: in the Editor Schedule() throws an exception.
cards/2/wrong/2: It works, but it is the slowest allocation, and nothing reminds you of a forgotten Dispose() after 4 frames.
cards/2/wrong/3: The allocator sets the lifetime, the checks, and whether the memory may go into a job at all.
cards/3/title: Temp inside a job — yes; main-thread Temp into a job — no
cards/3/body:
Allocating Allocator.Temp inside Execute is fine and encouraged: every job on every thread has its own Temp allocator, and everything allocated is released at the end of the job. It is the best choice for a temporary neighbour list, a traversal stack or an intermediate array — fast and leak-free.

The reverse is forbidden: main-thread Temp memory cannot be passed into a job. It is released at the end of the frame and the job may outlive the frame, so in the Editor Schedule() throws an exception. For data that goes into a job use TempJob or Persistent.
cards/4/explain: cells is allocated from main-thread Temp and passed into a job. In the Editor Schedule() throws an exception. Use TempJob (and Dispose after Complete) or a Persistent buffer allocated once.
cards/5/q: Match each allocator with its property
cards/5/pairs/0/1: No Dispose needed: released at the end of the frame or job
cards/5/pairs/1/1: For a job; free it within 4 frames
cards/5/pairs/2/1: A wrapper over malloc, lives until Dispose
cards/5/pairs/3/1: Cannot be passed into a job
cards/6/title: A long-lived buffer: allocate it once
cards/6/body:
A buffer you need every frame should not be allocated every frame. Even TempJob means an allocation and a free every frame, plus one more place to forget a Dispose().

The pattern: allocate Persistent once in Awake (or OnEnable), reuse it every frame, free it in OnDestroy (or OnDisable). On a NativeList, Clear() resets the length but keeps the capacity — no reallocation.

Before Dispose(), finish the pending job with Complete(): OnDestroy can arrive while this frame’s job has not been collected yet, and then the job would write into freed memory. IsCreated guards against a second Dispose() and against a buffer that was never allocated.
cards/7/task: Boids allocates a TempJob buffer in every Update and frees it in LateUpdate. Rework it: allocate velocities once in Awake with Allocator.Persistent, reuse it every frame and free it in OnDestroy — after Complete() on the pending job.
cards/7/checks/0/label: Awake allocates the buffer with Allocator.Persistent
cards/7/checks/1/label: There is no new NativeArray in Update
cards/7/checks/2/label: There is no Dispose() in Update or LateUpdate
cards/7/checks/3/label: There is an OnDestroy, and it calls Dispose()
cards/7/checks/4/label: In OnDestroy, Complete() comes before Dispose()
cards/7/explain: One allocation for the component’s whole life instead of an allocation and a free every frame, and a single place where the memory is freed. Complete() in OnDestroy is needed because this frame’s job may still be running: in the Editor the safety system catches a Dispose() under a live job, in a build the job would write into freed memory. In the interview: “long-lived buffers are Persistent, I allocate them in Awake and free them in OnDestroy after Complete”.
cards/8/title: Free it after the job: Dispose(JobHandle)
cards/8/body:
If a temporary buffer is only needed by jobs, there is no reason to wait on the main thread just to call Dispose(). Dispose(JobHandle) schedules the free as one more job that runs after the given one, and returns its JobHandle.

That way a TempJob buffer lives exactly as long as the chain that needs it, and the main thread never blocks. The old way is the [DeallocateOnJobCompletion] attribute on a job field: it still works, but only for NativeArray. For Collections containers use Dispose(JobHandle).
cards/9/title: Leak detection: where did it leak
cards/9/body:
Unity tracks native allocations and reports the forgotten ones. The level is in Edit > Preferences > Jobs > Leak Detection Level, or in code via NativeLeakDetection.Mode:

  • Disabled — no tracking;
  • Enabled — report leaks; this is the default in the Editor and in development builds, while a regular build defaults to Disabled;
  • EnabledWithStackTrace — also the call stack where the memory was allocated; it works only in the Editor and development builds, and capturing a stack for every allocation is expensive — turn it on while you hunt.

Forgotten memory is reported when the script domain unloads, not at the moment of the leak. So a report without a stack tells you little: switch to EnabledWithStackTrace, reproduce, and see where it was allocated. The “TempJob older than 4 frames” check works separately from this.
cards/9/deep: There are more allocators than the classic three. Allocator.Domain (in the engine since Unity 2023.1) lives as long as the script domain. Collections 2.x adds AllocatorManager and custom allocators such as RewindableAllocator: many allocations, then one fast rewind instead of many frees. In Entities a world has a WorldUpdateAllocator — a double buffer whose allocations live for two frames, need no manual free and can be passed into jobs.
cards/10/q: What is true about native memory leaks? Select all.
cards/10/options/0: The garbage collector will eventually free a forgotten NativeArray
cards/10/options/1: EnabledWithStackTrace shows where the leaked memory was allocated
cards/10/options/2: Dispose() on a Temp allocation does nothing
cards/10/options/3: Persistent gets the same lifetime check as TempJob
cards/10/options/4: In a regular (non-development) build, leak detection is off by default
cards/10/explain: Native memory is outside the managed heap; the GC never frees it. Only EnabledWithStackTrace gives you the allocation stack. Temp is released in full at the end of the frame or job, so Dispose() on it is a no-op. Persistent has no lifetime checks: a forgotten buffer only shows up as a leak at domain unload. A regular build defaults to Disabled.
cards/11/q: Interviewer: “Why not just allocate everything as Persistent and stop thinking about it?”
cards/11/options/0: Persistent is the slowest allocation with no lifetime checks. For short-lived buffers TempJob is faster and flags a forgotten Dispose after 4 frames, and for scratch data inside a job there is Temp. Persistent is for buffers you allocate once and reuse
cards/11/options/1: Persistent memory is slower to read and write in a job: it sits further from the cache than TempJob
cards/11/options/2: Persistent cannot be passed into a job — the safety system requires TempJob for all job data
cards/11/options/3: Persistent is freed by the garbage collector, and big buffers cause GC pauses
cards/11/explain: You choose an allocator by lifetime: inside a job — Temp, one-off into a job — TempJob, long-lived — Persistent, allocated once. Memory access speed does not depend on the allocator; what differs is the cost of allocating and the checks.
cards/11/wrong/1: Access is equally fast: Persistent is slow only at the moment of allocation.
cards/11/wrong/2: It can be, and long-lived job buffers usually are Persistent.
cards/11/wrong/3: The GC does not touch native memory at all — which is why you free it by hand.
